pumac-2012-finals-a-01.title: Take n = p - 3
pumac-2012-finals-a-01.body:
Since $p>5$, $p$ is coprime to $12,15,20$ and $p\ge7$, so $n=p-3\ge4$ is a positive integer. We claim $p\mid20^{p-3}+15^{p-3}-12^{p-3}$.

Note $\frac1{20^2}+\frac1{15^2}=\frac{9+16}{3600}=\frac{25}{3600}=\frac1{12^2}$, which is the same as $20^2=\frac{3600}{9}$, $15^2=\frac{3600}{16}$, $12^2=\frac{3600}{25}$. Write
$$20^{p-3}=\frac{20^{p-1}}{20^2}=\frac{9\cdot20^{p-1}}{3600},\quad15^{p-3}=\frac{16\cdot15^{p-1}}{3600},\quad12^{p-3}=\frac{25\cdot12^{p-1}}{3600}.$$
Since $9+16-25=0$, we can subtract $9+16-25$ copies of $1$:
$$20^{p-3}+15^{p-3}-12^{p-3}=\frac{9(20^{p-1}-1)+16(15^{p-1}-1)-25(12^{p-1}-1)}{3600}.$$
By Fermat's little theorem each of $20^{p-1}-1$, $15^{p-1}-1$, $12^{p-1}-1$ is divisible by $p$, so $p$ divides the numerator. The left side is an integer and $3600=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5^2$ is coprime to $p$, so $p$ divides the left side. ∎

pumac-2012-finals-a-01.title: Idea behind n = p - 3
pumac-2012-finals-a-01.body: Let $f(n)=20^n+15^n-12^n$. It satisfies $f(-2)=\frac1{400}+\frac1{225}-\frac1{144}=0$, and modulo $p$ the values $f(n)$ are periodic in $n$ with period dividing $p-1$. Hence $f(-2+(p-1))=f(p-3)\equiv0\pmod p$. The first solution makes this rigorous.

pumac-2012-finals-a-02.title: Tangent substitution
pumac-2012-finals-a-02.body:
The condition and the inequality are unchanged under $(a,b,c)\to(-a,-b,-c)$. Among $a,b,c$ two have the same sign; after possibly flipping all signs we may assume two of them, say $a,b$, are $\ge0$.

If $ab=1$, the condition gives $a+b=0$ (cancel $c$), impossible for $a,b\ge0$; so $ab\ne1$ and $c=\frac{a+b}{ab-1}$. Let $A,B\in[0,\frac\pi2)$ with $\tan A=a$, $\tan B=b$, and $C=\pi-A-B$. Then $A+B\ne\frac\pi2$ (as $ab\ne1$), and $\tan C=-\tan(A+B)=\frac{a+b}{ab-1}=c$.

Since $\frac1{\tan^2x+1}=\cos^2x$,
$$\sum\frac1{a^2+1}=\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C,$$
the last equality being the standard identity for $A+B+C=\pi$. (Check: $\cos^2C=(\sin A\sin B-\cos A\cos B)^2$, and expanding gives $\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-2\cos A\cos B\cos C$.)

It remains to show $\cos A\cos B\cos C\le\frac18$. As $\cos A,\cos B\ge0$: if $\cos C<0$ the product is $\le0$. Otherwise all three cosines are nonnegative; by AM-GM $\cos A\cos B\cos C\le\left(\frac{\cos A+\cos B+\cos C}3\right)^3$, and since $\cos$ is concave on $[0,\pi]$ (Jensen), $\frac{\cos A+\cos B+\cos C}3\le\cos\frac{A+B+C}3=\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12$. So the product is $\le\frac18$, and the sum is $\ge1-\frac14=\frac34$. ∎

pumac-2012-finals-a-03.title: Power of a point
pumac-2012-finals-a-03.body:
Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and let $T$ be the second intersection of line $AD$ with $\Omega$: the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$.

**Step 1: $T$ is the center of $\Gamma$.** We have $\angle TBI=\angle TBC+\angle CBI=\frac A2+\frac B2$ (as $\angle TBC=\angle TAC=\frac A2$) and $\angle TIB=\angle IAB+\angle IBA=\frac A2+\frac B2$ (exterior angle of $\triangle ABI$). So $TB=TI$, and similarly $TC=TI$. Thus $T$ is equidistant from $B,I,C$, i.e. $T$ is the center of $\Gamma$. In particular $TP=TQ$.

**Step 2: $A,P,T,Q$ are concyclic.** $D$ lies on chord $BC$ of both $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$, so it is inside both circles. Chords $BC$ and $PQ$ of $\Gamma$ meet at $D$: $DP\cdot DQ=DB\cdot DC$. Chords $BC$ and $AT$ of $\Omega$ meet at $D$: $DB\cdot DC=DA\cdot DT$. Hence $DP\cdot DQ=DA\cdot DT$, with $D$ between $P$ and $Q$ and between $A$ and $T$; by the converse of the intersecting chords theorem, $A,P,T,Q$ lie on a circle $\omega$. (If $PQ=BC$ this still holds with $\{P,Q\}=\{B,C\}$.)

**Step 3: angles.** $A$ and $T$ are on opposite sides of line $PQ$ (since $D\in PQ$ lies between them), so $T$ lies on the arc $PQ$ of $\omega$ not containing $A$. The chords $TP$ and $TQ$ of $\omega$ are equal, so they subtend equal inscribed angles at $A$: $\angle PAT=\angle TAQ$. As $T$ lies on line $AD$, $AD$ bisects $\angle PAQ$. ∎
